title: The Mapping Problem: From Question to Table to Answer

events.narration: In the last lesson, we watched AI return three completely different revenue numbers for the exact same question. That wasn't a glitch. That was the system working exactly as designed — just against the wrong table. And here is the thing: that problem doesn't only affect revenue. It affects every business question you ask against a schema that hasn't been documented properly. In this lesson I want to show you exactly what that looks like across two different business questions. We're going to run each question twice — against two different tables — and you're going to see the numbers diverge every single time.

Take a look at the schema panel on the left side of your screen. You can see eight tables in this database. Accounts, churn events, customers, monthly metrics, order details, order summary, orders, and subscriptions. Now notice something — several of these table names overlap in meaning. Customers and accounts both sound like they store customer information. Monthly metrics and churn events both sound like they track churn. This is the mapping problem. When you ask a question in plain language, AI has to choose which table to query. And without documentation, that choice is essentially a guess. Let me prove it to you right now.

I've prepared four queries in this SQL file. Two for our first business question, two for our second. Each pair asks the identical question but targets a different table. We're going to run them one at a time and watch what happens. The first business question is this: how many active customers do we have right now? Sounds simple. But watch carefully.

There's our result. You can see the column is called active customers, and the value is one hundred and fifty-eight. This query went to the customers table and counted every row where status equals active. One hundred and fifty-eight. Remember that number. Now I'm going to ask the exact same question — word for word, same logic — but point it at the accounts table instead. Watch what happens.

One hundred and forty-three. Not one hundred and fifty-eight. That is a difference of fifteen customers — for the exact same question. So which one is right? Well, both queries are technically correct SQL. The issue is that these two tables contain different data. The customers table holds only paying customers. The accounts table holds two hundred and ten total records — customers, prospects, and leads combined. But only one hundred and forty-three of those have a status of active. The customers table, by contrast, holds only verified paying customers, and one hundred and fifty-eight of them are active. Neither table has a comment, a description, or any documentation that explains this difference. If AI picks accounts, you report one hundred and forty-three. If AI picks customers, you report one hundred and fifty-eight. Both answers look completely reasonable. One of them is wrong for your use case.

Now we're on our second business question: what was our churn rate in Q3? This result came from the monthly metrics table, which stores pre-calculated rates by month. You're looking at three rows — one for each month in Q3 of 2024. July shows zero point zero five. August shows zero point zero two five. September shows zero point zero two. These are decimal representations of percentages. So July was roughly five percent churn, August three percent, September two percent. These numbers were calculated by whoever built this table and stored here as a summary. Now here's the question: is there another way to calculate churn from this same database? There is. There's a churn events table with individual records for every customer who churned. Let's run the same question against that table instead.

Here's what the churn events table gives us for the same Q3 period. Five churn events recorded in Q3 total. The calculated rate is zero point zero two five — meaning roughly two and a half percent of our two hundred customers churned. Now compare that to the monthly metrics table. July alone showed zero point zero five — roughly five percent. The churn events table gives a blended Q3 rate of about two point five percent, but the monthly metrics table shows higher rates for individual months. These are measuring different things. Monthly metrics may be calculating churn based on a different formula, a different customer base, or a different time window. We genuinely don't know — because nothing is documented. This is exactly the situation your AI tool is navigating every time someone asks about churn. It picks a table. It runs a query. It returns a number. The number looks precise. It may be measuring the wrong thing entirely.
Now let me bring all four results together so you can see the full picture side by side.

There it is. Four queries. Two business questions. And every single one returns a different answer. Query one and query two ask how many active customers we have — one hundred and fifty-eight versus one hundred and forty-three. Query three and query four ask about Q3 churn — and they return numbers calculated from completely different sources. This is not a bug. This is what happens when you have a warehouse full of tables that overlap in meaning, with no documentation to explain what each one actually contains. AI doesn't know which answer you need. It can't know — unless you tell it. And the way you tell it is through proper data design, clear naming conventions, and documentation. That is what this course is about.

In the next lesson, we're going to trace one of these failures all the way through a real workflow. We'll follow a business question from the initial ask, through the AI query, all the way to the number that lands in a board presentation. And you'll see exactly what the cost looks like when this kind of ambiguity goes undetected. I'll see you there.
